items.prompt: Which part of your skeleton protects your brain?

options.why: Your ribs protect your heart and lungs.
Your backbone holds you up and lets you bend.
Your kneecap protects your knee.

hints: Your brain is inside your head.
Which bone forms a hard case around your head?
Gently tap the top of your head. What is under your hair?
items.explanation: Your skull is a hard case of bone around your brain. It protects your brain from bumps.

items.prompt: Match each part of the skeleton to its job.
pairs: holds the body upright and lets it bend
hints: Think about where each part is in your body.
Bones that make a cage or case protect soft organs.
Start with the skull. What is inside your head?
items.explanation: The skull protects the brain, and the ribs protect the heart and lungs. The backbone holds you upright and lets you bend.

items.prompt: Choose 3 jobs of the human skeleton.

options.why: Your stomach and intestines digest food.
Your heart pumps blood.

hints: Imagine your body with no bones at all.
Think about the skull and the ribs.
Remember that muscles pull on bones to move you.
items.explanation: The skeleton supports the body and protects organs such as the brain and heart. Muscles pull on bones so the body can move.

items.prompt: Sort the animals by their skeleton.
hints: Some animals have bones inside. Some have a hard case outside.
Insects, crabs and spiders have a hard outer covering.
Start with the earthworm. Can you feel any hard parts?
items.explanation: Cats, fish and birds have bony skeletons inside. Beetles, crabs and spiders have exoskeletons outside, and earthworms and jellyfish have no skeleton.

items.prompt: A hard covering on the outside of an insect's body is called an ___.
hints: Insects have no bones inside.
This covering is a skeleton on the outside.
The word starts with exo, which means outside.
items.explanation: An exoskeleton is a hard covering outside the body. It supports and protects animals such as insects, spiders and crabs.

items.prompt: A crab grows too big for its exoskeleton. What happens next?

options.why: An exoskeleton is hard. It cannot stretch.

options.text: It sheds the old one and grows a bigger one.

options.why: Crabs keep growing. They shed their old covering to do it.

options.text: Bones grow inside the crab instead.
options.why: A crab has no bones inside. Its skeleton is on the outside.

hints: An exoskeleton is hard, like a suit of armour.
Think about what you do when your shoes are too small.
Could hard armour stretch as you grow?
items.explanation: A hard exoskeleton cannot grow. The crab sheds it, and a new, bigger one hardens in its place.

options.why: Spiders have an exoskeleton and no backbone.
Earthworms have no bones at all.
Ants have an exoskeleton, not a backbone.

hints: A backbone is part of a skeleton inside the body.
Insects and spiders have their skeleton on the outside.
Which animal has bones you could feel through its skin?
items.explanation: A frog has a skeleton inside its body, with a backbone. Animals with a backbone are called vertebrates.

items.prompt: About how many bones are in an adult human skeleton?

options.why: That is far too few. Each hand alone has 27 bones.
There are more. Your hands and feet have over 100 bones between them.
That is far too many. The real number is about one tenth of that.

hints: Your hands and feet alone have lots of small bones.
The number is more than 100 but less than 1000.
The hands and feet have over 100 bones. Then add the rest of the body.
items.explanation: An adult skeleton has about 206 bones. More than half of them are in the hands and feet.

items.prompt: A newborn baby has more bones than an adult. Why?

options.text: Adults lose bones when they fall over.
options.why: A fall can break a bone, but the bone heals. It is not lost.

options.text: Some bones drop out as children grow.
options.why: Bones do not drop out like milk teeth.

options.text: Adult bones shrink until they disappear.
options.why: Bones grow as you grow. They do not disappear.

options.text: Some small bones join together as a child grows.

hints: The bones do not leave the body.
Think about what happens to the skull as a baby grows.
Two small bones could become one big bone. How?
items.explanation: A newborn baby has nearly 300 bones. As a child grows, some of them join together, so an adult has about 206.

options.why: Your skull protects your brain.
Your kneecaps protect your knees.
Your eyes sit in bony holes in your skull.

hints: Your ribs are in your chest.
Which organs are inside your chest?
Feel your chest as you breathe in. What is moving?
items.explanation: Your ribs make a cage around your heart and lungs. The cage protects them and moves as you breathe.

items.prompt: A turtle has a hard shell on its back. It also has a backbone inside. Which group is it in?

options.text: animals with an exoskeleton, because of its shell
options.why: The shell is joined to the skeleton inside. A turtle has a backbone.

options.text: vertebrates, because it has a backbone

options.why: A turtle has bones inside its body.

options.text: invertebrates, because it has a shell
options.why: Invertebrates have no backbone. A turtle has one.

hints: Do not be tricked by the shell.
The groups are about the backbone.
Read the second sentence again carefully.
items.explanation: A turtle has a backbone, so it is a vertebrate. Its shell is made of bone and is joined to its skeleton.

items.prompt: Draw a simple human skeleton. Label the skull, ribs and backbone.

criteria.label: Draws a skull, ribs and backbone in the right places

hints: Start with the skull at the top.
Draw the backbone down the middle, then the ribs around the chest.
items.explanation: The skull sits at the top, the backbone runs down the middle of the back and the ribs curve around the chest.

items.prompt: Draw your arm on paper. Label the bones you know, such as the upper arm bone and the lower arm bones. Then take a photo.
hints: Your arm has bones inside it.
items.explanation: Your tutor checks that the arm and its bones are drawn and labelled.
